```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(wfmR)
library(ggplot2)
wfm_chart_defaults()

mtcars_cyl <- transform(mtcars, cyl = factor(cyl), gear = factor(gear))

category_df <- data.frame(
  group = factor(
    tools::toTitleCase(names(wfm_palette())),
    levels = tools::toTitleCase(names(wfm_palette()))
  ),
  value = c(31, 27, 24, 21, 18, 16, 13)
)

volcano_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(volcano))
names(volcano_df) <- c("x", "y", "height")
volcano_df <- transform(
  volcano_df,
  x = as.integer(x),
  y = as.integer(y),
  signal = height - mean(height)
)

wide_vehicle_table <- data.frame(
  Model = row.names(mtcars),
  Cylinders = mtcars$cyl,
  Gears = mtcars$gear,
  Transmission = ifelse(mtcars$am == 1, "Manual", "Automatic"),
  `Miles per gallon` = sprintf("%.1f", mtcars$mpg),
  `Weight (1000 lbs)` = sprintf("%.2f", mtcars$wt),
  `Gross horsepower` = mtcars$hp,
  `Quarter-mile time` = sprintf("%.2f", mtcars$qsec),
  `Rear axle ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", mtcars$drat),
  Displacement = sprintf("%.0f", mtcars$disp),
  check.names = FALSE
)
wide_vehicle_table <- wide_vehicle_table[
  order(wide_vehicle_table$Cylinders, wide_vehicle_table$Gears, wide_vehicle_table$Model),
]
row.names(wide_vehicle_table) <- NULL

air_df <- data.frame(
  year = floor(as.numeric(time(AirPassengers))),
  month = factor(month.abb[cycle(AirPassengers)], levels = month.abb),
  passengers = as.numeric(AirPassengers)
)

wfm_demo_table <- function(
  x,
  caption,
  label,
  align = NULL,
  col.names = NULL,
  notes = NULL,
  source = NULL,
  latex_resize = FALSE
) {
  note_html <- if (!is.null(notes) || !is.null(source)) {
    paste0(
      "\n<div class=\"chart-notes figure-notes\"><p>",
      if (!is.null(notes)) paste0("<em>Notes:</em> ", notes) else "",
      if (!is.null(notes) && !is.null(source)) "<br>" else "",
      if (!is.null(source)) paste0("<em>Source:</em> ", source) else "",
      "</p></div>\n"
    )
  } else {
    ""
  }

  note_latex <- if (!is.null(notes) || !is.null(source)) {
    paste0(
      "\n\\par\\nopagebreak[4]\\vspace{0.35em}",
      "\\begingroup\\raggedright\\footnotesize\\linespread{0.88}\\selectfont\\itshape{}",
      if (!is.null(notes)) paste0("Notes: ", notes) else "",
      if (!is.null(notes) && !is.null(source)) "\\\\\n" else "",
      if (!is.null(source)) paste0("Source: ", source) else "",
      "\\par\\endgroup\n"
    )
  } else {
    ""
  }

  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    body <- knitr::kable(
      x,
      format = "latex",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      align = align,
      col.names = col.names,
      row.names = FALSE
    )
    if (isTRUE(latex_resize)) {
      body <- paste0("\\resizebox{\\textwidth}{!}{%\n", body, "\n}")
    }
    cat(body, note_latex, sep = "\n")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }

  body <- knitr::kable(x, align = align, col.names = col.names, row.names = FALSE)
  knitr::asis_output(paste0(body, note_html))
}
```

# Overview

This article demonstrates the shared HTML and PDF defaults in `wfmR`. The HTML
render uses the default system sans-serif stack, while the PDF render uses the
LaTeX defaults from the package extension.

The examples use ggplot2 [@wickham2016ggplot2] and the built-in `mtcars`,
`AirPassengers`, and `volcano` datasets, so the demo can render anywhere the
package is installed. The grammar-of-graphics framing follows
@wilkinson2005grammar, while the prose uses ordinary Quarto markdown. Generic
coloured labels such as [salmon]{.label-salmon}, [teal]{.label-teal},
[purple]{.label-purple}, and [lime]{.label-lime} inherit the note highlight
style.

::: {.course-note}
Use `mainfont` under `wfmr-html` only when a paper-like HTML note should read
closer to the PDF output. Leave it unset for the default sans-serif article
style.
:::

The report style is intentionally more editorial than the academic style.
Chart titles and subtitles sit above the image, notes and sources sit below,
and the surrounding page uses the soft Rose Pine-inspired palette for links,
labels, tables, and callout accents.

This expanded demo deliberately references each chart and the single table from
nearby prose. In the HTML render those references become hoverable links. In the
PDF render they provide a useful check that floats remain close to the paragraph
that introduces them.

# Palette

The primary palette is ordered for categorical charts: salmon, teal, purple,
lime, yellow, blue, and pink. Each base colour also has named tints from
90 to 10 percent of the original colour. The palette is intentionally softer
than publication-first categorical schemes, but it still follows the general
principle that colour choices should be documented rather than left implicit
[@brewer2003colorbrewer].

@fig-category-bars uses every default colour. It is a simple diagnostic
for checking the categorical order in HTML, PDF, and revealjs output. It also
gives the PDF renderer an early figure reference before enough prose has
accumulated to force a difficult page break.

Dummy placement text follows the first reference so the PDF renderer has a
choice to make. The text is deliberately content-light: it exists to fill the
page between the cross-reference and the float, letting the chart move to the
bottom of the current page or the top of the next page. In normal analysis this
space would describe the sample, the measurement choices, and the reason the
diagnostic appears before the substantive plots.

```{r}
#| label: fig-category-bars
#| chart-title: "The default palette supports larger categorical charts"
#| chart-subtitle: "Seven bars use the primary wfmR order"
#| chart-notes: "The full seven-colour set is useful for brand consistency; for analytical comparisons, direct labels remain preferable when categories are dense."
#| chart-source: "Illustrative data."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
category_df |>
  ggplot(aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_wfm() +
  scale_y_wfm(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, subtitle = "Value") +
  theme_wfm() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Chart Metadata

The chart metadata hook lets chunks use `chart-title`, `chart-subtitle`,
`chart-notes`, and `chart-source` rather than hand-building captions. The
rendered caption and notes stay consistent across HTML, PDF, and revealjs. This
section uses two chart shapes to check that the metadata works across common
report objects. @fig-scatter introduces a bivariate pattern, and @fig-boxplot
changes the geometry while keeping the same caption structure.

These objects are not intended as a substantive vehicle analysis. They are
small, portable examples that make cross-references, captions, subtitles, notes,
sources, and legends visible in a single document. That is useful
because visual hierarchy is easiest to judge when the same object appears in
ordinary surrounding prose, not only in isolated screenshots. The same logic is
behind the classic advice to use graphics as part of the argument rather than as
decoration [@cleveland1993visualizing; @tufte2001visual].

This paragraph is another placement spacer. It is intentionally mundane and
repetitive, because the point is to create the conditions under which LaTeX has
to decide whether the next figure belongs at the bottom of the current page or
the top of the next page. The object should not remain inline merely because it
was inserted at this point in the source.

A second spacer paragraph makes the test more obvious in the generated PDF. In
a real report it might discuss robustness checks, modelling assumptions, or
data cleaning decisions. Here it simply gives the float queue enough surrounding
text to reveal whether the theme is using genuine top and bottom floats.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| chart-title: "Fuel economy is lower for heavier cars"
#| chart-subtitle: "A small example using the built-in mtcars dataset"
#| chart-notes: "The fitted line is illustrative. Colours come from the wfmR primary palette."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(wt, mpg, colour = cyl)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.88) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "#2F2F33",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_colour_wfm(name = "Cylinders") +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(
    x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
    y = NULL,
    subtitle = "Miles per gallon"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boxplot
#| chart-title: "Fuel economy also varies by transmission gearing"
#| chart-subtitle: "Boxplots provide a second categorical chart example"
#| chart-notes: "Groups are small because this is the built-in mtcars dataset."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(gear, mpg, fill = gear)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.62, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_wfm() +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(x = "Forward gears", y = NULL, subtitle = "Miles per gallon") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Distribution Checks

The next pair of objects puts a more crowded chart near the only table in the
demo. @fig-density checks whether overlapping fills, legend keys, and axis
labels remain quiet enough for report prose. @tbl-wide-vehicles is deliberately
wide, with enough rows and columns to test HTML table styling and PDF float
placement without filling the document with repeated table examples.

The goal is practical rather than statistical. If a theme works only for one
bar chart and one tiny summary table, it will not survive normal project work.
Distribution plots, a wide table, and nearby narrative text create a better
stress test for spacing and cross-reference behaviour.

This dummy paragraph is here to push the next figure away from its first
reference. The desired behaviour is not inline placement. The desired behaviour
is a top or bottom float that remains close enough to the reference while
keeping the surrounding text block readable.

The same stress test applies to the following table. A table emitted as
`longtable` cannot float, so the PDF version of this demo now emits a real
LaTeX `table` environment. The table is wide enough to exercise scaling in PDF
and horizontal breathing room in HTML, while still remaining one grouped object
with its caption, notes, and source.

```{r}
#| label: fig-density
#| chart-title: "Fuel economy distributions are visibly different by cylinder count"
#| chart-subtitle: "Density curves test alpha blending, legends, and axis spacing"
#| chart-notes: "The curves are illustrative and use the small built-in mtcars data."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 7.3
#| fig-height: 4.1
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(mpg, fill = cyl, colour = cyl)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_wfm(name = "Cylinders") +
  scale_colour_wfm(name = "Cylinders") +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(x = "Miles per gallon", y = NULL, subtitle = "Density")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wide-vehicles
#| tbl-cap: "Wide vehicle summary for table placement"
#| results: asis
wfm_demo_table(
  wide_vehicle_table,
  caption = "Wide vehicle summary for table placement",
  label = "tbl-wide-vehicles",
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  notes = "The table is intentionally wide and uses all 32 cars so that PDF placement and scaling remain visible.",
  source = "R datasets package.",
  latex_resize = TRUE
)
```

# Time Series

The built-in `AirPassengers` series gives the article demo a non-vehicle
example and a different visual rhythm. @fig-air-trend uses the sequentially
ordered time index. The example is useful for checking that figure placement
remains sensible after the earlier wide table has already entered the float
queue.

The line chart also checks that the palette can support a single primary
accent without making every graphic look like a categorical palette showcase.
This is the report counterpart to a typical short empirical note: a trend, a
few paragraphs explaining why the object is present.

The next two dummy paragraphs are deliberately ordinary. They create a page
where the time-series figure can plausibly fit at the bottom, but may need to
move to the top of the following page if the accumulated caption and notes make
that impossible. This is the sort of case where an inline figure would leave an
awkward hole in the prose.

The extra prose remains here to keep testing placement pressure after the table
section. The cross-reference should do the navigational work, while LaTeX
handles whether the figure sits at the top or bottom of a nearby page.

```{r}
#| label: fig-air-trend
#| chart-title: "Passenger counts rise sharply in the late 1950s"
#| chart-subtitle: "Monthly totals from the built-in AirPassengers series"
#| chart-notes: "The example is included to exercise a time-series chart in the same theme."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.0
air_df |>
  ggplot(aes(year + (as.numeric(month) - 1) / 12, passengers)) +
  geom_line(colour = wfm_palette()[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_point(colour = wfm_palette()[["salmon"]], size = 1.4, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL, subtitle = "Passengers")
```

# Continuous Scales

Sequential and diverging scales are derived from the primary colours and their
tints using OKLab interpolation. @fig-sequential and @fig-diverging
use the same matrix so that the sequential and diverging palettes can be
compared directly. This final section is deliberately placed after several
other floats so the PDF output has enough material to reveal whether later
figures still attach themselves to nearby references.

One last dummy paragraph creates space before the continuous-scale figures. The
final two charts should still remain above or below nearby text rather than
slipping after the references. The barrier before the bibliography is retained
only to prevent unresolved floats from entering the reference list.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sequential
#| chart-title: "Sequential colour uses a derived wfmR scale"
#| chart-subtitle: "Blue, teal, and pale yellow encode ordered values"
#| chart-notes: "The palette is sampled with OKLab interpolation."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.7
ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x, y, fill = height)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_wfm_seq(palette = "blue_teal_yellow", name = "Height") +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_wfm(grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-diverging
#| chart-title: "Diverging colour centres the substantive zero"
#| chart-subtitle: "Teal and salmon sit on either side of a neutral midpoint"
#| chart-notes: "Use the midpoint argument when zero or another reference value has substantive meaning."
#| chart-source: "R datasets package."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.7
ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x, y, fill = signal)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_wfm_div(palette = "teal_salmon", midpoint = 0, name = "Signal") +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_wfm(grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```
